pages.title: How to calculate and review restaurant prime cost
pages.heading: How to calculate and review restaurant prime cost
pages.description: Calculate restaurant prime cost from cost of goods sold, full labor cost and sales for the same period. Check the inputs before interpreting the percentage.
pages.author: Ready Margin
pages.keyword: How to calculate and review restaurant prime cost
pages.takeaway: Prime cost is cost of goods sold plus labor cost, divided by sales for the same period. It measures major operating costs, not final profit.

sections.title: Use costs and sales from the same period
sections.body: Prime cost combines cost of goods sold and labor cost. Divide that combined amount by sales for the same dates and multiply by 100. Agree the accounts included, the labor-cost basis and the inventory treatment with the person preparing the report.

sections.title: Example calculation
sections.body: In a fictional reporting period, cost of goods sold is $18,000, labor cost is $22,000 and sales are $70,000. Prime cost is $40,000, or about 57.1% of sales. This calculation illustrates the method; it is not a target or a Ready Margin customer result.

sections.title: Check completeness before comparison
sections.body: Late invoices, different payroll dates and incomplete inventory counts can alter the ratio. Identify estimates and use comparable cutoffs before comparing this period with another.

sections.title: Investigate food and labor separately
sections.body: An overall percentage does not identify the cause. Review supplier prices, usage and sales mix for food cost; compare planned hours, attendance and full employment costs for labor. Set a working target around your restaurant’s format and operating plan.

pages.seoTitle: How to calculate and review restaurant prime cost

pages.title: Restaurant month-end close checklist
pages.heading: Restaurant month-end close checklist
pages.description: Use a restaurant month-end checklist for settlements, bank accounts, supplier invoices, payroll and reporting. Assign each input and unresolved question.
pages.author: Ready Margin
pages.takeaway: A restaurant close needs reconciled accounts, complete period costs and identified exceptions, with someone responsible for every missing input.

sections.title: 1. Agree the period, close date and contacts
sections.body: Name the person supplying each statement and answering each type of question. Confirm the bank, card, POS, payroll and inventory sources required for the month.

sections.title: 2. Reconcile sales and account activity
sections.body: Compare POS totals, card and delivery settlement statements and bank receipts. Keep fees, refunds and timing differences with their source references. Investigate unexplained amounts.

sections.title: 3. Check costs that belong to the month
sections.body: Review supplier bills, credits, payroll entries and stock count dates. Ask the person preparing the accounts how costs are treated when the supporting document arrives late.

sections.title: 4. Review and deliver the reports
sections.body: Check unusual balances and incomplete inputs. Present the agreed statements with material changes and a dated list of unresolved items. The close is ready for review only when its completeness and limitations are understood.

pages.title: Restaurant recipe costing: units, yield and portions
pages.heading: Restaurant recipe costing: units, yield and portions
pages.description: Calculate restaurant recipe costs from current pack prices, usable quantities and portion sizes. Check kitchen practice before using the result for pricing.
pages.author: Ready Margin
pages.keyword: Restaurant recipe costing: units, yield and portions
pages.takeaway: Recipe costing depends on current prices, comparable units, usable yield and the portion actually served.

sections.title: Confirm the recipe being served
sections.body: Write down ingredients, sauces, garnishes and batch components with the kitchen. Record the working portion and date. A recipe file that differs from actual preparation will produce an unreliable comparison.

sections.title: Convert pack prices into usable unit costs
sections.body: Record purchase quantity and the amount usable after preparation. For example, a fictional $30 pack yielding 6 kilograms has a usable cost of $5 per kilogram. A portion using 150 grams of that ingredient costs $0.75 before other ingredients.

sections.title: Calculate the batch and portions
sections.body: Multiply each usable unit cost by its recipe quantity, add the ingredients and divide by the batch’s usable portions. Retain the invoice reference and the kitchen-confirmed yield.

sections.title: Use the result with sales mix and operating costs
sections.body: Ingredients are one cost of serving the dish. Labor, waste, overhead and sales mix also affect the business result. Investigate changed prices or portions before management changes the menu.

pages.title: How to reconcile restaurant delivery payouts
pages.heading: How to reconcile restaurant delivery payouts
pages.description: Reconcile restaurant delivery-platform sales, fees, refunds and bank deposits. Keep settlement references and timing differences with the accounting record.
pages.author: Ready Margin
pages.keyword: How to reconcile restaurant delivery payouts
pages.takeaway: A delivery payout should be traced to the sales, fees, refunds and adjustments on its settlement statement.

sections.title: Start with a settlement statement
sections.body: Identify the platform, statement dates, payout reference and expected deposit date. Retain the original statement so the net receipt can be reconstructed.

sections.title: Separate gross activity from the net receipt
sections.body: In a fictional example, $1,000 of sales less $200 of fees and $50 of refunds produces a $750 receipt. The accountant confirms how each component is recorded; the bank deposit alone does not describe gross sales.

sections.title: Match the receipt and explain timing
sections.body: Compare the statement reference and payout date with bank activity. A deposit arriving in a later period may be a timing difference; an unexplained deduction requires investigation.

sections.title: Carry exceptions into the close
sections.body: List missing statements and unexplained amounts with the contact supplying the answer. Resolve them or identify the limitation before presenting the period’s accounts.

pages.seoTitle: How to reconcile restaurant delivery payouts

sections.title: Keep the approved version and completion evidence

sections.title: Review changes with the responsible adviser

pages.title: How to build a restaurant cash review
pages.seoTitle: How to build a restaurant cash review
pages.heading: How to build a restaurant cash review
pages.description: Build a restaurant cash review from dated balances, expected receipts and payment obligations. Label estimates and update the plan before major commitments.
pages.author: Ready Margin
pages.keyword: How to build a restaurant cash review
pages.takeaway: Cash planning depends on when receipts arrive and obligations fall due, as well as their total amounts.

sections.title: Define the period and opening position
sections.body: Choose the horizon needed for the decision and date the included bank balances. Confirm receipts already settled and commitments already authorized.

sections.title: List money expected and money due
sections.body: Use settlement statements for expected receipts and approved records for payroll, bills and other obligations. Record dates as well as amounts; distinguish confirmed entries from assumptions.

sections.title: Example of a timing gap
sections.body: In a fictional week, a $5,000 balance faces $4,000 of payments before an expected $3,000 settlement arrives. The timing matters even if the week’s total receipts exceed its payments. Confirm the dates before deciding what is available.

sections.title: Review and update before acting
sections.body: Uncertain receipt dates and incomplete bills can change the plan. Explain those limits alongside any scenarios. A forecast is an estimate, not a guarantee or evidence of funds received.

pages.title: How to review restaurant labor cost
pages.seoTitle: How to review restaurant labor cost
pages.heading: How to review restaurant labor cost
pages.description: Review restaurant labor cost using full employment costs, sales, scheduled shifts and attendance for comparable dates. Confirm the operating explanation.
pages.author: Ready Margin
pages.keyword: How to review restaurant labor cost
pages.takeaway: A labor-cost comparison needs consistent cost definitions and dates, verified hours and the context of the shifts.

sections.title: Agree the cost and sales basis
sections.body: Define included wages, payroll taxes, benefits and other employment costs with the report preparer. Use the same dates for costs and sales. Schedule estimates based on base wages are a different measure.

sections.title: Compare planned and recorded hours
sections.body: Match shifts and attendance for the period. Ask managers about cover, training, longer service or an early finish. Confirm missing time records before interpreting the difference.

sections.title: Separate volume and cost changes
sections.body: A labor percentage can rise when sales fall even if hours are unchanged. Compare both amounts and the operating week before recommending a response.

sections.title: Choose a management action and review date
sections.body: A finding may call for a correction, a shift-pattern review or a change in the input process. Management determines staffing and pay with appropriate advice.

pages.heading: Example: a missing clock-out before payroll.
pages.description: A fictional restaurant payroll example shows how the original punch, manager confirmation and approval handoff stay connected before cutoff.

sections.title: The exception
sections.body: An employee has a recorded start but no finish time. The schedule lists a planned finish, which cannot establish the hours actually worked.

sections.title: The confirmation
sections.body: The preparation team asks the shift manager what happened and checks the available time record. The confirmed correction retains its reason and source.

sections.title: The approval handoff
sections.body: The nominated approver receives the prepared input and any question still open at cutoff. This is a fictional process example, not evidence of a completed customer payroll run.

sections.body: A familiar delivery has a higher invoice total. The receiving contact checks whether quantities, item specifications or substitutions changed.

sections.title: The price check
sections.body: The review compares unit prices and any agreed credit. A different case size may explain the total; an unexplained difference goes to the supplier contact.

sections.title: The documented response
sections.body: The confirmed explanation stays with the bill. Management decides whether to approve payment or request a correction. The example does not claim achieved savings.

pages.title: Why restaurant sales and available cash differ
pages.heading: Why restaurant sales and available cash differ
pages.description: Understand how settlements, fees, refunds and payment dates separate restaurant sales from cash available. Review the relevant statements and commitments.

sections.title: Sales, settlements and deposits measure different stages
sections.body: Sales show trading activity. A settlement statement explains what the processor will pay after relevant fees or adjustments. The bank records the amount that arrived and its date.

sections.title: Timing can cross the reporting period
sections.body: A weekend’s card or delivery sales may settle after the sales period ends. Check actual provider statements rather than assuming every sale immediately appears in the account.

sections.title: Existing commitments affect the amount available
sections.body: Payroll, approved bills and other obligations may be due before the next receipt. List them beside the dated balance and identify any estimates.

sections.title: Use both views in the financial review
sections.body: The P&L and the cash review answer different questions. Ready Margin can review the records and timing behind each; management decides on payments and spending.

pages.takeaway: Sales describe trading; available cash depends on settled receipts and the obligations due before the next receipt.

pages.title: Restaurant payroll cutoff checklist
pages.heading: Restaurant payroll cutoff checklist
pages.description: Check restaurant pay-period dates, attendance exceptions, tip records and the final approved version before payroll cutoff. Assign each unresolved input.

sections.title: 1. Confirm the dates and the input cutoff
sections.body: Schedules, attendance, tips and corrections must cover the intended pay period. Confirm when prepared inputs must reach the approver and processor.

sections.title: 2. List exceptions with the confirming contact
sections.body: Identify missing punches, changed shifts, rate questions and unmatched tips. Include the shift or check reference and the manager responsible for the answer.

sections.title: 3. Confirm the approval route
sections.body: The nominated person needs the reviewed inputs and a clear statement of unresolved items. Decide with the responsible provider how an exception received after cutoff is handled.

sections.title: 4. Verify the final version
sections.body: Check that authorized corrections reached the file or record handed to payroll. Retain the original input, reason and confirmation; do not assume a discussion automatically changed the final record.

pages.takeaway: Before cutoff, check the dates, exceptions, approver and final version—not just whether an input file exists.
pages.author: Ready Margin

pages.title: Why restaurant food cost changes between periods
pages.heading: Why restaurant food cost changes between periods
pages.description: Investigate a restaurant food-cost change through comparable dates, unit prices, counts, recipes and sales mix. Confirm the cause with source records.

sections.title: Check whether the comparison is consistent
sections.body: Compare the same dates and account definitions. A late invoice or a count taken on a different day can shift the reported result.

sections.title: Separate purchase price from usage
sections.body: Check supplier pack sizes and unit prices, then examine quantities used between counts. Recipes, yield, portions and waste records can explain usage where they are available.

sections.title: Include the dishes being sold
sections.body: A change in sales mix can alter the average ingredient cost. Review current menu and sales records before attributing the movement to a kitchen or supplier problem.

sections.title: Verify the strongest explanation
sections.body: Ask the kitchen or purchasing contact for the record that would confirm the suspected cause. Management then chooses a specific response and a measure to review.

pages.takeaway: Food-cost movement can come from prices, usage, sales mix or reporting timing. Confirm the cause before choosing a change.

pages.title: Restaurant attendance checks before payroll
pages.heading: Restaurant attendance checks before payroll
pages.description: Compare restaurant schedules, punches and manager-confirmed changes before payroll preparation. Keep corrections traceable to the original shift record.

sections.title: Use the schedule to locate the exception
sections.body: Compare the planned shift with recorded start and finish times. A changed shift may be legitimate; the schedule provides context rather than proof of the worked hours.

sections.title: Ask the manager to confirm the work
sections.body: Record the shift reference, question and person supplying the answer. Preserve the original punch and the reason for any correction.

sections.title: Identify what remains unresolved at cutoff
sections.body: The approver should know which input is missing, who is investigating and the relevant deadline. Follow the process agreed with the payroll provider for late answers.

sections.title: Review repeated corrections
sections.body: Recurring missing punches may point to a timekeeping or manager handoff problem. Discuss that process at the next cycle while keeping individual pay questions documented.

pages.takeaway: The manager’s confirmation and correction reason should stay attached to the original attendance record.

pages.title: Restaurant supplier invoice review checklist
pages.heading: Restaurant supplier invoice review checklist
pages.description: Check restaurant invoices against orders, deliveries, quantities, pack sizes and credits. Route discrepancies before the payment decision.

sections.title: Collect the order, receiving record and invoice
sections.body: Identify the item references, quantities and missing documents. Ask the receiving contact to confirm substitutions or shortages.

sections.title: Compare units before comparing price
sections.body: A changed pack size may explain a higher invoice total. Compare the unit price and delivered quantity, then check credits and agreed pricing.

sections.title: Send each discrepancy to the responsible person
sections.body: The restaurant confirms receipt; the supplier answers price and credit questions. Retain the responses with the invoice and keep disputed amounts identified.

sections.title: Present the bill for approval
sections.body: The authorized person decides on payment. Keep approval status distinct from payment evidence, then carry the relevant bill information into the accounts and cash review.

pages.takeaway: A supplier bill review compares the order, delivery and invoice, and distinguishes approval from completed payment.

pages.title: Five checks for a restaurant weekly P&L review
pages.heading: Five checks for a restaurant weekly P&L review
pages.description: Check dates, cost completeness and operating context before interpreting a restaurant weekly P&L. Use the findings to assign a specific next action.

sections.title: 1. Confirm the dates and comparison
sections.body: Different trading-day counts or payroll cutoffs can distort the movement. State the dates covered and the basis of the comparison.

sections.title: 2. Identify provisional costs
sections.body: Late invoices, estimated stock or incomplete payroll records affect the result. Ask which amounts may change when the final input arrives.

sections.title: 3. Trace the material movement
sections.body: Review changes in sales, food, labor and overhead separately. Use supporting entries to distinguish timing differences from a change in operations.

sections.title: 4. Ask managers about the week
sections.body: Service changes, covers, delivery issues and menu mix may explain the figures. Record the relevant context beside the financial comparison.

sections.title: 5. Assign a check or decision
sections.body: Name the person, required record and next date. A weekly report should lead to a specific investigation or management decision where the evidence supports one.

pages.takeaway: A useful weekly P&L states its dates and completeness, explains the material changes and identifies the next check.

pages.title: How to compare restaurant location performance
pages.heading: How to compare restaurant location performance
pages.description: Compare restaurant sites with consistent accounts, reporting dates and allocations. Keep local format, trading hours and missing records in the explanation.

sections.title: Agree the common reporting basis
sections.body: Use consistent periods, account definitions and treatment of shared costs. Document entity coverage and inter-location transfers before combining results.

sections.title: Check whether every site’s records are complete
sections.body: A missing invoice at one site can make its margin look stronger. Identify provisional inputs and the date they will be updated.

sections.title: Retain the local operating differences
sections.body: Format, hours, capacity and recent changes can explain results. A common reporting structure should make those differences easier to examine.

sections.title: Turn the comparison into local questions
sections.body: Ask the relevant manager about a specific finding and source record. Review the answer before treating a group average as a target for every location.

pages.takeaway: Align the reporting definitions across locations, then explain the operating differences that remain.

sections.body: Where online delivery is enabled, the form sends the enquiry through the configured delivery service. An email option is available if delivery fails. On the static review website, the form prepares an email draft for you to send.

sections.title: Optional analytics
sections.body: Analytics are off unless you allow them. On the Vercel-hosted website, allowing measurement enables Vercel Web Analytics and Speed Insights. Reported page URLs omit query strings and fragments; form values and checklist answers are excluded.

sections.title: Preferences and questions
sections.body: You can change optional measurement through Cookie choices in the footer. For questions about an enquiry or the handling of your information, contact contact@readymargin.com.

pages.takeaway: Read how Ready Margin uses enquiry details and stores website preferences. Optional analytics require your choice and can be changed from the footer.

sections.title: Information about the service
sections.body: This website describes Ready Margin’s services and provides general operating information. A separate agreement establishes the work, responsibilities, timing and fees for any engagement.

sections.title: Demonstrations and examples
sections.body: The public workspace uses sample records and disconnected providers. Workflow examples are fictional and do not represent customer results. No particular profit, savings or recovery outcome is guaranteed.

sections.title: Website materials
sections.body: Ready Margin’s text, artwork and other materials carry their applicable rights and licences. Contact us before reproducing branded materials.

sections.title: Questions about an engagement
sections.body: Confirm contracting terms and professional responsibilities in the separate service agreement. Questions about this website can be sent to contact@readymargin.com.

sections.title: Preferences stored in your browser
sections.body: The website can store your analytics choice and display preferences. These support the browsing experience and are not used to identify you across websites.

sections.title: Measurement is optional
sections.body: Optional analytics remain off until you select Allow. Events are sent only when a measurement provider is connected and your current choice permits them.

sections.title: Changing your choice
sections.body: Select Cookie choices in the footer to reopen the controls. Rejecting measurement stops future optional events; it does not erase information already received by a provider.

sections.title: Navigation and controls
sections.body: The website provides a skip link, labelled controls and visible keyboard focus. Menus and product tabs can be operated with a keyboard.

sections.title: Display and motion preferences
sections.body: Layouts adapt to narrow screens and text can be enlarged. Reduced-motion preferences and the static mode limit movement for visitors who need them.

sections.title: Report a browsing barrier
sections.body: Email contact@readymargin.com with the page and difficulty encountered. You can include your browser or assistive technology to help explain the issue.

sections.title: Ongoing improvements
sections.body: Accessibility is reviewed as the website changes. This statement describes the controls provided and does not claim independent certification or compatibility with every setup.

faqs.question: Which restaurant finance jobs can you handle?
faqs.answer: We can quote for bookkeeping, accounting, payroll preparation, tip records, supplier bills, cost review and CFO support. The proposal specifies the tasks and outputs included.

faqs.question: Am I buying software or a service?
faqs.answer: Ready Margin is a managed finance service supported by a workspace. Our team performs the work in your agreement. The public workspace demonstrates the process with sample data.

faqs.question: Can we use our existing POS, payroll and accounting systems?
faqs.answer: We review your current setup first. Access, exports and any direct connection must be verified before the service depends on them.

faqs.question: What happens in the free demo?
faqs.answer: We discuss your workload and show the relevant preparation or review process. You can ask about deliverables, approvals and fees before requesting a proposal.

faqs.question: How do you calculate the price?
faqs.answer: We assess your locations, transaction and payroll workload, record condition and chosen support. The written quote separates recurring service from cleanup, specialist work and third-party costs.

faqs.question: Do I need to send financial records before the demo?
faqs.answer: No. System names, current responsibilities and one example are enough. Detailed records can follow after the sharing arrangements are agreed.
